claims.statement: JFrog documents the Artifactory API key as a per-user secret introduced in Artifactory 4.4.3, states that the API key is deprecated from Artifactory 7.47.x, and states that API keys start with AKCp.

sources.supports: "API Keys follow this pattern: .*\bAKCp[A-Za-z0-9]{69}\b.*, starting with AKCp"; API Keys introduced in Artifactory 4.4.3, never expire, can be retrieved from a database
sources.locator: section "Comparing Identity Reference Tokens With API Keys"

sources.supports: "From Artifactory 7.47.x, the API Key is being deprecated."
sources.locator: Create API Key description (deprecated: true)

claims.statement: Gitleaks (jfrog.go) and TruffleHog (artifactory detector), maintained separately, both treat a JFrog API key as a 73-character alphanumeric value: Gitleaks as a keyword-gated rule for a 73-character alphanumeric run, TruffleHog as the literal AKCp prefix followed by 69 alphanumeric characters. This agrees with the length stated by the provider page for the AKCp form and is not the provider's rule.

sources.supports: rule jfrog-api-key uses a 73-character alphanumeric capture, gated by the keywords jfrog, artifactory, bintray, xray

claims.statement: JFrog's API Key page states that an API key authenticates REST API calls in two ways: in the X-JFrog-Art-API header, or as the password of basic authentication with the username (instead of the account password).

sources.supports: Artifactory allows authentication for REST API calls using your API key as an alternative to your username and password in two ways: either by using the `X-JFrog-Art-API` header with which you can specify an API key, or through basic authentication using your username and API key (instead of your password).
sources.locator: API Key, introduction

claims.statement: JFrog's API Key page states that API keys are saved in the database and can be retrieved through the REST API or the UI, are created without an expiry date and by default never expire, and that a single user has one active API key at a time.

sources.supports: API Keys are retrievable: the keys are saved in the database and can be retrieved via REST API or the UI. ... since API Keys are not created with an expiry date, and, by default, never expire ... A single user can have a single active API Key at any moment
sources.locator: JFrog API Key Deprecation Process, Why Is JFrog Deprecating API Keys

claims.statement: JFrog states that API keys were introduced in Artifactory 4.4.3 and that a key must have been generated with Artifactory 4.4.3 or later to authenticate; a key generated before 4.4.3 must be regenerated and the new key used as the basic-authentication password.

sources.supports: To use your API key for authentication, it must be generated using Artifactory 4.4.3 or later. If generated prior to 4.4.3, you **must** regenerate your API key and use the new key as a password for basic authentication.
sources.locator: Artifactory Minimum Supported Version

sources.supports: When JFrog introduced API Keys in Artifactory 4.4.3, the API Keys provided users with a solution to easily create a secret.
sources.locator: Comparing Identity Reference Tokens With API Keys

It describes API key deprecation as a process in which JFrog has begun the countdown to fully discontinuing support for the feature.

claims.statement: Two JFrog-maintained client repositories, jfrog-client-go and build-info (one maintainer, so one origin), each identify an API key by the leading characters AKCp8 together with a length of at least 73 characters; the Go client then sends such a value as the basic-authentication password rather than as a Bearer token. The code states no maximum length and no alphabet, and the fifth character 8 is narrower than the AKCp prefix on the documentation page.

notes: Project-authored by the Redact Secret project, which maintains this repository; not independent evidence. Draft; not yet reviewed. Revised in place as a draft on 2026-10-06 by an AI agent run (credential-evidence#246): claims and open questions added, the stale existence-only question removed because the family is now researched, the two earlier open questions api-key-format-conflict and api-key-temporality-period rewritten to the current state of the evidence (the latter replaced by final-authentication-shutdown-not-stated, end-of-life-meaning and release-dates-for-artifactory-versions). Existing claims are untouched.

openQuestions.question: Which form applies to which Artifactory releases is unresolved. The pattern statement (AKCp plus 69 alphanumerics, 73 characters), JFrog's two client repositories (prefix AKCp8, at least 73) and two independent scanner rule artifacts are consistent with a 73-character AKCp form, while the Create API Key example (44 characters, base64 punctuation, no AKCp) is stated by the same provider and has been published unchanged since at least 2025-09-06. Settled by a JFrog statement of the key format per release, or the example being declared schematic; an issued sample is issuance-gated and was not sought.

The client code names AKCp8 and the documentation names AKCp. Whether AKCp keys exist with another fifth character, and what the fifth character encodes, is not stated by any page read. Public repositories hold other AKCp-leading strings of unknown origin; they were not used.

No page read states a release or date at which authentication with an existing API key stops unconditionally. The pages state deprecation (7.47.x), an End of Life notice (end of Q4 2024), creation disabled (7.98) and an administrator-controlled usage block that is off by default (7.107.1 and the self-hosted flag). Deprecation, end of new-key issuance and final shutdown are separate facts and only the first three are documented. Settled by a JFrog release note or lifecycle statement that names a shutdown release or date.

The page says the API key has reached End of Life and, on the same page, describes usage blocking as an optional administrator setting that is off by default. Whether End of Life means the end of support or the end of authentication is not stated. Settled by a JFrog definition of the term for this feature.

The pages date the lifecycle only by Artifactory release (4.4.3, 7.47.x, 7.47.10, 7.84.x, 7.98, 7.107.1) and by the quarter of the End of Life notice. The calendar dates of those releases are not on the pages read; a JFrog release-notes source would settle them. No historical period is asserted on a validity field.
The pages describe cloud and self-hosted controls separately and do not state whether the cloud platform applied the creation block or the End of Life on the same dates as self-hosted releases.
